questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was seen with a 4-month history of worsening gait disturbance, slurred speech, and mood swings. She had been low in mood and quick tempered and was sleeping poorly. This had not responded to a trial of antidepressant therapy. There had been no preceding illness or other associated symptoms. On physical exam, she demonstrated choreiform movements together with an ataxic gait. Detailed neuropsychologic assessment demonstrated impairment of memory, spatial judgment, verbal fluency, and language. She was not able to give the date or year. A diagnosis of new variant CJD was considered.
questions.lead_in: What test is most likely to be diagnostic?

options.text: EEG for pseudo-periodic sharp wave activity
Genotyping for codon 129 of the PrP gene

questions.explanation: Tonsil biopsy for PrPSC immunostaining PrPsc immunostaining of tonsillar tissue is both sensitive and specific for vCJD and avoids more invasive procedures such as a brain biopsy. EEG changes and CSF 14-3-3 protein may be negative in vCJD; they are more useful in classic CJD. MRI changes in vCJD tend to show bilateral pulvinar hyperintensity. Cortical ribboning is seen with classic CJD. Genotyping for codon 129 of the PrP gene confirming methionine/methionine homozygosity would be interesting but would not confirm the diagnosis of vCJD.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q11

questions.stem: A 51-year-old man presented with several months of rapidly progressive cognitive decline and new onset tremors. He was previously healthy and has no family history of neurocognitive disorders. Four months ago, he was able to work and function normally. He has had behavioral changes and memory impairment, and most recently has started to have gait instability and tremors. EEG showed periodic sharp waves and T2-weighted MRI showed increased activity in both thalamic nuclei. A lumbar puncture was performed and routine tests were ordered.
questions.lead_in: Which nonroutine study would you consider adding to help elucidate the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Immunoassay for 14-3-3 protein This patient likely has Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. He has had rapidly progressive cognitive decline with extrapyramidal symptoms. Classic EEG pattern with CJD includes periodic sharp-wave activity. Brain MRI showed the “pulvinar sign” with increased thalamic activity bilaterally. Elevated levels of 14-3-3 protein in the CSF would be supportive of a diagnosis of CJD, though it can be elevated in a variety of other conditions, including other viral encephalitides and stroke. Quiz 8 Answers
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q33

questions.question: Infection prevention and control measures for a surgical case in suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

parts.text: What are the infection prevention and control measures for a surgical case in suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

parts_raw.text: What are the IPC measures for a surgical case in suspected CJD?

questions.model_answer: a) Standard precautions suffice for routine patient care; most body fluids including blood can be handled with standard precautions, while special precautions are recommended for handling CSF. For the surgical/neurosurgical setting: (1) Use single-use/disposable instruments wherever practicable to eliminate the need for reprocessing, quarantine, and tracking. (2) Reusable neurosurgical instruments exposed to high-infectivity tissue (brain, spinal cord, dura, posterior eye, pituitary) must be either discarded or decontaminated by prion-specific reprocessing, since routine sterilization does not inactivate prions. (3) Prion-specific reprocessing means prolonged steam autoclaving, or a combination of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) soak followed by autoclaving. (4) The hospital should have guidelines for handling, quarantine, and tracking of instrument sets used on patients biopsied for dementia or undiagnosed neurodegenerative illness, so instruments can be traced and quarantined pending diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell gives the principle but refers to Chapter 299 for detailed decontamination; the specific CDC/WHO/PHAC protocols (e.g., immersion in 1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite then autoclave at 121°C, incineration of high-infectivity disposables, tissue infectivity categories) come from those guidelines, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: CDC/WHO - Disposable material: should be disposed of by incineration if come in contact with high infectivity tissue (brain, cord, eye). Heat-Sensitive material: Soak in 2N NaOH or undiluted sodium hypochlorite for 1 hour then rinse with water. Heat resistant material: if come in contact with high infectivity or low infectivity tissue (CSF, kidneys, lung, liver, lymph nodes, spleen, placenta): Immerse in 1N NaOH and autoclave at 121 C for 30 minutes; rinse, routine sterilization. Immerse in 1N NaOH or bleach (sodium hypochlorite: 20,000 ppm) for 1 hour, then autoclave at 121 C for 1 hour. Clean, then routine sterilization. Repeat step 2. Number of cases documented from instruments: 6. (Notes: Can the instruments tolerate CJD decontamination? if yes, CJD decontaminate & reuse; if no, routine reprocessing separately & quarantine. Is diagnosis of CJD excluded? if yes, reuse; if no, discard.)

questions.question: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

parts.text: What are guidelines for surgical screening?
If biopsying the brain of a suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease patient, what 4 things do you tell the surgeon?
What should the hospital do to ensure a proper approach (3 things)?

parts_raw.text: What are guidelines for surgical screening?
If biopsying a brain of suspected CJD patient, what 4 things do you tell the surgeon?
What should the hospital do to ensure proper approach (3 things)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Before elective neurosurgery/brain biopsy for dementia or an undiagnosed neurodegenerative illness, perform a risk assessment to determine whether additional precautions are required, based on the patient's CJD risk category, the procedure planned, and whether high- versus low-infectivity tissue will be contacted. Screen for iatrogenic risk factors (dura mater or corneal grafts, cadaveric human growth hormone/gonadotropin, prior neurosurgery) and family history of prion disease.
b) (1) Use single-use/disposable instruments where practicable so they can be discarded rather than reprocessed. (2) Any reusable instruments contacting high-infectivity tissue (brain, dura, spinal cord) must undergo prion-specific decontamination (prolonged autoclaving or NaOH plus autoclaving) or be discarded, because routine sterilization does not inactivate prions. (3) Minimize the number of instruments and personnel involved and, where possible, schedule the case last. (4) Label, track, and quarantine the instrument set pending the diagnosis so it is not returned to general use.
c) (1) Establish a specific institutional policy/committee for CJD instrument handling consistent with published (PHAC/WHO/CDC) guidance. (2) Ensure a defined reprocessing/quarantine and tracking procedure for neurosurgical instruments. (3) Educate surgeons, nurses, and all involved staff on the policy and ensure a risk assessment is applied to elective and emergency cases.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell supports the principles (risk-based assessment, disposable instruments, prion-specific reprocessing, quarantine/tracking, and hospital guidelines, with detail deferred to Chapter 299); the itemized surgical-screening and biopsy checklists derive from the PHAC (2007) Classic CJD Quick Reference Guide.

cohort_answer.text: PHAC (2007) - Classic CJD in Canada Quick Reference Guide. Perform risk assessment to determine if additional precautions required based on: risk category of patient; procedures performed; high vs low infectivity tissue. For biopsy: perform surgery as last case of day if possible; involve minimum number of healthcare personnel; limit number of instruments used; use single-use equipment if possible; if reusable, label/track instrument sets, ensure they tolerate decontamination; store/dispose in Biohazard-marked container; avoid mixing high and low infectivity instruments; after procedure - high infectivity tissue: discard equipment; low infectivity tissue: decontaminate by cleaning thoroughly, soaking in sodium hydroxide, rinsing, sterilizing in autoclave; no infectivity tissue: routine reprocessing/reuse. Hospital should ensure: 1) committee and specific policy to prevent CJD per PHAC guidelines; 2) universal sterilization procedure for neurosurgical instruments; 3) surgeons/nurses/all healthcare personnel up to date on policy, with risk assessment for elective/emergent surgery patients.

questions.question: A patient with suspected prion disease and a subdural hematoma has a brain biopsy. They call you to ask what should be done with the surgical/operating room instruments.
questions.question_raw: A patient with suspected prion disease and a subdural hematoma has a brain biopsy. They call you to ask what they should do with the surgical/OR instruments.

parts.text: What should be done with the surgical/operating room instruments?

parts_raw.text: What should be done with the surgical/OR instruments?

questions.model_answer: a) Do not return the instruments to routine reprocessing. Because a brain biopsy contacts high-infectivity tissue (brain, and dura in a subdural case), the instruments must be either discarded or subjected to prion-specific decontamination — prolonged steam autoclaving, or a combination of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) soak followed by autoclaving — since standard sterilization does not inactivate prions. In practice, quarantine/track the set pending confirmation of the diagnosis; if CJD is confirmed, discard high-infectivity items (or reprocess by the prion protocol only if the instruments tolerate it), and use single-use instruments in the first place where practicable to avoid this problem.
questions.beyond_mandell: The tissue-infectivity categories (high: brain, CSF, dura, pituitary, posterior eye, spinal/trigeminal ganglia; low: cornea, kidney, liver, lung, lymph node, placenta, spleen) and detailed reprocessing steps are from CDC/WHO/PHAC guidance (Mandell Chapter 299), not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: High infectivity tissue: discard equipment. Low-infectivity tissue: decontamination by cleaning thoroughly, soaking in sodium hydroxide, rinsing, sterilizing in autoclave. Not infective: routine reprocessing/reuse. Highly infectious tissue: Brain, CSF, dura, pituitary, posterior eye, spinal cord/ganglia, trigeminal ganglia. Low-infectivity: Cornea, kidney, liver, lung, lymph node, placenta, spleen. Not infective: all else.
